title: Describing a noun: words before a noun
summary: Any engine can turn white and describe a noun: verbs, い-adjectives, noun + だ (the な form), and the の car.

blocks.text: You already know three kinds of engine: a **verb** (う-train), a **noun + だ** (だ-train) and an **い-adjective** (い-train). Each of them can also be turned into a **white engine**: a describing word that sits **in front of a noun** and cannot pull a train by itself. It simply tells you more about the noun behind it.
An い-adjective is already in the right shape. Put it in front of the noun.
赤いペンが小さい。 The red pen is small.
2. Verbs: whole clauses can describe a noun
A verb in any tense can describe the noun that comes after it, and so can everything attached to the verb. Build it in two steps: first a normal sentence, then move the verb in front of its noun.
歌った少女が寝ている。 The girl who sang is sleeping.
Anything the verb brings along comes with it. The same trick works with a thing that was acted on: the dictionary can be the one that was eaten, or the dog can be the one who ate.

blocks.en: the dog that ate the dictionary
the dictionary that the dog ate

blocks.text: A copula engine (noun + だ) turns into **な** in front of a noun. Words that behave this way are called な-adjectives (textbooks) or adjectival nouns. They are nouns of a special class, which is why they need だ as an engine.
やんちゃな犬が寝ている。 The naughty dog is sleeping.
Now you can read the long sentence from section 2 with a な-adjective engine at the end.

blocks.jp: 辞書を食べた犬がやんちゃだ。
blocks.en: The dog that ate the dictionary is naughty.

blocks.text: An ordinary noun describes another noun with **の**. It works like English 's, and it can also name the class something belongs to: in the example below, a dress of the class "pink". You do not have to memorize which nouns take の and which take な. You will pick it up from exposure, and a wrong choice is only a small mistake.
さくらのドレスが新しい。 Sakura's dress is new.

items: **い-adjective** straight in front of the noun: **赤いペン**.
